extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers and storytellers learning story structure and scene craft
extracted.subtask_description: Using Dwight V. Swain's scene-sequel model (scene = goal/conflict/disaster; sequel = reaction/dilemma/decision) as a structuring tool for entire story acts and major story movements. Advice and examples on how each beat maps to common act phases (e.g., Ordinary World, Call to Adventure, Denial, Crossing the Threshold).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene: goal, conflict, disaster
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenes are an action-based progression of goal, conflict, and disaster.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The protagonist pursues a desire (goal). Opposition threatens the ability to obtain that desire (conflict). When conflict peaks, a "logical, yet unanticipated development" ends her plans in disaster. Scenes should create the question "What will the protagonist do now?" and grip audiences with forward motion. (Example: Luke's ordinary-world goal and the escalating incident with the droid.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequel: reaction, dilemma, decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Sequels are the response progression of reaction, dilemma, and decision following a disaster.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the shock of the disaster, the protagonist must process what happened, take stock, and form a new plan. Sequels show the protagonist's decision-making and internal processing and must be compelling in their own right. They convert emotional reaction into a new goal that restarts the cycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the sequel's process difficult (best-bad choice)
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist's decision should be a hard choice—a crisis of "best bad choice" or a "choice between equally unsatisfactory alternatives."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequels are about hard moral/strategic dilemmas; the protagonist should not arrive at an easy, clean solution. Use the tension of irreconcilable goods to create stakes in the decision phase. (Cites Shawn Coyne and Swain.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance action and response (scenes vs sequels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good stories balance gripping action-scenes with emotionally resonant sequels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scenes grip with suspense about what happens next; sequels allow emotional and logical resonance to strike home. Both are necessary: action provides momentum, response provides meaning. Treat both as equally important parts of pacing and structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply scene-sequel at act level (act beats as scene/sequel)
rubrics_metrics.description: Swain's scene-sequel framework, though focused on individual scenes, can be applied to whole act structures and major story movements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map an act's major phases to repeated cycles of goal → conflict → disaster → reaction → dilemma → decision. Use this to structure first acts, mid-builds, or the second half of Act 2 (Act 2b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary World = goal & conflict (prior goal)
rubrics_metrics.description: The opening (Ordinary World) maps to the scene phases of goal and conflict, often representing a 'prior' goal that hints at deeper needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The early goal should manifest the protagonist's desire and hint at her need rather than being the story goal. Example: Luke's desire to escape his boring life and attend the Imperial Academy—an ordinary-world goal that foreshadows larger needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Call to Adventure = disaster (status quo disrupted)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Call to Adventure functions as the disaster beat: a radical upset of the protagonist's status quo that forces a reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At this disaster moment the protagonist can no longer continue with former plans and must confront the plot's demands. Example: Obi-wan's rescue/invitation to Luke that makes his former life impossible to continue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial/Debate = reaction & dilemma (processing the disruption)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Denial of the Call (or Snyder's 'Debate') maps to the sequel's reaction and dilemma phases where the protagonist processes and resists the change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humans need time to absorb abrupt events; the protagonist must integrate implications, offer excuses, and struggle through indecision. Often a final catalyst (a minor disaster or revelation) is needed to force a decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision = crossing the threshold (new story goal)
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision phase corresponds to Crossing the First Threshold: the protagonist forms a new goal and commits to the main plotline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This choice launches the main story goal and completes the scene-sequel cycle for that act. Example: Luke deciding to go with Obi-wan after discovering his aunt and uncle were killed—his former life is destroyed and he must move forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeat the cycle across major movements (e.g., Act 2b: All Is Lost → Dark Night → Recommitment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The scene-sequel cycle should repeat for each major story movement, not just individual scenes or the first act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the framework for subsequent larger beats: e.g., Act 2b's disaster becomes an All Is Lost moment, the sequel becomes a Dark Night of the Soul, and the decision becomes a Recommitment that sets the protagonist toward climax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the framework as a tool, not an absolute rule
rubrics_metrics.description: No framework is perfect; some stories succeed despite breaking the scene-sequel form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat scene-sequel as another story-tool in your kit. Apply it where it helps and ignore or adapt it where a story benefits from flouting the pattern.
